questions.question: Generated passwords: the spec says printable ASCII. Should the generator leave out the space (validation still accepts spaces)?

options.label: No space (Recommended)
options.description: Generate from 0x21-0x7E, default 12 characters, clamped to the entry's locks' range. A space at either end is invisible on screen and easy to mistype on a keypad.

options.label: Printable ASCII incl. space
options.description: Exactly as the spec says, 0x20-0x7E.

questions.question: The slot card has one reveal toggle per card, so revealing to edit the PIN also sends the password in cleartext to the browser. Keep it card-wide?

options.label: Card-wide (Recommended)
options.description: One reveal for the card; masked display shows only the active tab. Same trust boundary as today's PIN reveal.

options.label: Per type
options.description: Reveal takes a list of types, so revealing the PIN doesn't send the password. More code in the websocket and both cards.

questions.question: What happens to the existing generate_pin action, which users' automations and the wiki's guest examples call?

options.label: Keep it, add generate_credential (Recommended)
options.description: generate_pin stays unchanged forever (one registration); generate_credential(type, length, optional entry) is the general action the card uses.

options.label: Deprecate it
options.description: Add generate_credential, raise a deprecation repair for generate_pin, remove it in the next major release.

questions.question: PR 3 maps to about 13 tasks: websocket payloads, a generator, blueprints, then three cards. Split it?

options.label: Split: 3a backend, 3b cards (Recommended)
options.description: 3a: per-type sync helper, websocket payloads, get_config_entry_data types/ranges, generate_credential, blueprints. 3b: slot card, add-user card, lock card (TS + rebuilt bundle). Each reviewable on its own; 3a is all Python.

options.label: One PR 3
options.description: Everything together, as the spec's PR order says.

content.text:
That's correct: the length check runs first for every type. All five fixes are right.

The five review fixes for [#1772](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1772) are committed locally but not pushed. The full suite and `prek` pass, apart from the three timing-sensitive tests that flake in parallel and pass on their own.
- The text platform's lock-removed handler now ignores unloads.
- A password of only spaces is refused.
- Leftover `pin_required` repairs keep their text.
- The older flat form of `add_user` accepts `password`.
- A stale comment is fixed and one check is simplified.

PR 3 is split as you chose. I recorded your four decisions in the spec:
- generated passwords leave out the space;
- the slot card keeps one reveal toggle for all types;
- `generate_pin` is deprecated with a repair, in favor of `generate_credential`;
- 3a is the Python backend, 3b the three cards.

The worktree `.worktrees/password-cards` is now on branch `feat/password-cards-backend`, stacked on #1772's latest commit.

The research raised several things the 3a plan has to handle:
- **Per-type sync state has to come from the sync engine, not entities.** The per-type in-sync sensors are disabled by default, so the websocket can't read their states.
- **Password edits currently push no update to the cards.** The websocket subscription doesn't track the password entity yet.
- **The add-user card can't learn the entry's credential types or length ranges.** It needs a new field on an existing websocket command.
- **3b will need two leak guards.** The slot card shows Home Assistant's error text, which quotes any value over 255 characters, so its password input needs a 255-character limit. It also trims what you type, which must stop for passwords.
- **Two blueprints assume PINs.** The usage limiter counts only PIN uses, and the credential-used blueprint doesn't list `password`.

An agent is drafting the 3a plan in the 2b plan's format. I'll review it when it finishes, before anything is implemented.

Shall I push the five fixes to #1772 and update its description?

input.prompt:
Give an independent design review of **PR 3b: the dashboard cards for password credentials** in Lock Code Manager (a Home Assistant custom integration with Lit/TypeScript cards). The project owner suspects the current design needs a rethink. Your job is to judge that on the merits, not to defend the existing design. **Read only; do not edit repository files.** Write your review to `/tmp/lcm-pr3/3b-design-review.md`.

**Background.**
- Lock Code Manager keeps users' credentials in sync on their locks.
- Until now each user had a PIN. PR 2b (#1772, branch `feat/password-config`) adds an optional **password** per user, beside the PIN. A user needs at least one of the two.
- Only some locks take passwords: Z-Wave User Credential locks (a later PR) and the Virtual test lock. **Most installs will have PIN-only locks for the foreseeable future.**
- Each lock keeps the credential types it takes; an entry offers the union across its locks.

**The current design** is in the spec `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-password-credential-design.md`: the "Cards" section, decisions 8, 9, 10, 13 and 14, and "Services and websocket". In short:
- **Slot card:** tabs per credential type between the name and the value row; each tab has a sync dot; only the value field changes per tab.
- **Add-user card:** the same tabs on its credential input, with a generator per type.
- **Lock card:** type tabs. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab lists managed users' passwords on that lock.
- **No tabs** when only one type is available.

**The code as it is today** (read it; cite file:line):
- worktree `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/password-cards`;
- `ts/slot-card.ts`, `ts/add-user-card.ts`, `ts/lock-codes-card.ts`, their styles, `ts/shared-styles.ts`, `ts/types.ts`, the strategies (`ts/dashboard-strategy.ts`, `ts/slot-section-strategy.ts`, `ts/lock-section-strategy.ts`, `ts/generate-view*.ts`);
- the websocket payloads in `custom_components/lock_code_manager/websocket.py`.

A code map with file:line citations is in `/tmp/lcm-pr3/research.md`, sections 2, 3, 6 and 7. Use it for orientation, and check what matters yourself.

**Constraints:**
- Dashboard cards can't use HA's form components, because an unregistered `ha-*` element renders as nothing. See `ts/no-mwc-components.test.ts`, `ts/dashboard-safe-elements.test.ts` and `ts/ha-components.ts` for what is allowed.
- No credential value may reach an error banner, a log or the masked payload. Home Assistant refuses a text value over 255 characters with the value in its error, and the slot card shows `err.message`.
- A password is kept as typed; a PIN is stripped.
- The reveal toggle stays card-wide (decision 14).
- PIN-only installs must look and behave exactly as today.

**Evaluate:**
1. **The tabbed slot card.** Is it the right UX for one user with up to two credentials? Consider at least:
   - (a) tabs, as specced;
   - (b) one stacked row per credential type, each with its own value, edit and sync dot, where PIN-only shows exactly one row as today;
   - (c) any better option you see.

   Weigh: discoverability (a hidden tab hides a credential's state), at-a-glance sync state, mobile width, accessibility, code size in `slot-card.ts` (already about 1555 lines), the `_editingField` state machine, test burden, and how each scales if more types (RFID, NFC) arrive later.
2. **The lock card's Password tab.** Is a per-lock password list needed at all, given the slot card shows each user's password and its per-lock sync? What does the lock card exist for today: unmanaged codes, empty positions, a per-lock overview? Does a password list fit that purpose? Options include a tab, a separate section below, a per-user line inside the existing chips, or leaving passwords off the lock card entirely for now.
3. **The add-user card.** Tabs over one credential input, or two plain fields (PIN, Password) shown only when the entry offers passwords? Consider the generator per type, and validation (at least one credential).
4. **What the backend (PR 3a) should send for your recommended design.** 3a is being planned now. Its current direction:
   - `subscribe_code_slot` gains `available_types` (PIN first) and `credentials: {type: {value | length, in_sync, state, min_length, max_length}}`, keeping the top-level `pin`/`pin_length`;
   - `subscribe_lock_codes` gains `credential_types` and `credentials.password: [...]`;
   - `get_config_entry_data` gains the entry's types and ranges.

   Say which of these your design needs, which it doesn't, and what's missing. This matters: 3a's plan can still change.
5. **Anything in the overall approach** that looks wrong or overbuilt for a feature only a minority of installs can use.

**Output** (`/tmp/lcm-pr3/3b-design-review.md`):
- a verdict: keep the specced design, adjust it, or rethink it;
- a recommended design per card, concrete enough to plan from;
- the alternatives you rejected, with one-line reasons;
- the 3a payload changes;
- risks.

Ground every claim about current behavior in code you read, with file:line. Don't invent behavior. Keep it decision-ready; it doesn't need to be long. Your final message should summarize the verdict and the top recommendations in under 20 lines.

input.summary: Revise 3a plan for the no-tabs card design
input.message:
Good plan. Raman has since adopted a different card design for 3b, so 3a's payloads change. Read `/tmp/lcm-pr3/3b-design-review.md` (the design review he adopted) and the revised spec decisions 8 and 9 in `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-password-credential-design.md`. **There are no tabs on any card.**
- **Slot card:** one row per credential type, each with its own value and sync state. While one row is edited, the others stay masked.
- **Lock card:** no Password tab. Each managed chip gets a one-line password status (set / not set / its sync state), with no value and no reveal.
- **Add-user card:** two plain fields; Password is shown only when the entry offers passwords.

Revise the plan in place (`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-25-password-pr3a-card-backend.md`):

1. **No length ranges in any payload.** Drop `min_length`/`max_length` from `subscribe_code_slot.credentials` and from `get_config_entry_data`. `get_config_entry_data` gains only an ordered `credential_types` list (PIN first). Keep the generator's clamping to the entry's locks (decision 15 keeps the optional entry, and Z-Wave PINs do have ranges), and keep the bounds helper Task 2 shares with the coordinator's length check. Drop `credential_length_range` if nothing else needs it.
2. **`subscribe_code_slot`:** keep `available_types` (PIN first), `entities.password` with tracking (your isolated tracking test is good), and the top-level `pin`/`pin_length`. `credentials[type]` carries `value | length` and the per-type sync status. Drop `in_sync` if the status alone tells the card what it needs; decide from what the slot card renders today and say which.
3. **`subscribe_lock_codes`:** replace the separate `credentials.password` list with per-slot (per-chip) credential states on the existing `slots` rows. Something like `credentials: {pin: REDACTED}, password: REDACTED, configured: bool}}`, sent only on locks that take more than PIN, so a PIN-only lock's payload is unchanged. **It also fixes a bug:** today a chip's `in_sync` comes from the slot's combined in-sync sensor (`websocket.py:664-667`, consumed at `lock-codes-card.ts:732-740` and `:779-781`), so on a password lock a pending password marks the PIN as pending. On a lock that takes more than PIN, the chip's PIN-facing `in_sync` (and anything the proxy-code logic reads) must come from the PIN's own state via your shared sync helper. Add a test on the Virtual entry that fails on today's code: a pending or held password with an in-sync PIN shows the PIN chip in sync. Keep `slots` byte-identical on PIN-only locks, and test that too.
4. **The deprecation repair and the card:** the add-user card keeps calling `generate_pin` until 3b, so on this branch alone every dashboard generate raises the repair. That's acceptable, since 3a and 3b ship in the same release. Note it in the plan and in the 3b carryover.
5. Update the "Payloads 3b reads" contract, the file map and the plan's decisions to match. Remove anything now unused (no dead fields). Keep the mutation checks honest for every changed test.

Report the revised task list, and every change from your previous version, one line each.

2057:## For 3b (from 3a, 2026-10-25)
## Decisions this plan makes (raise with Raman if any is wrong)

Raman's decisions (2026-10-25) are taken as given:
- 3a is backend only.
- Generated passwords are 0x21-0x7E, default 12, clamped into the entry's locks' range.
- Reveal stays card-wide.
- `generate_pin` is deprecated with a repair.
- No tabs on any card (decisions 8 and 9 revised): no length ranges in any payload, and per-chip credential states on the lock card instead of a password list.

Beyond those:

1. **No payload carries a length range; the generator still clamps.**
   - `credential_length_bounds(entry, type)` lists each entry lock whose cached capabilities give a range for the type. That is exactly the set `_validate_credential_length` checks today (`slot_coordinator.py:362-383`), which now iterates it.
   - `credential_length_range(entry, type)` intersects those bounds for the generator, its only caller.
     - It is `None` when the entry does not offer the type.
     - Its minimum is the largest lock minimum (0 when no lock says), and its maximum the smallest lock maximum, capped at 255 (`MAX_LENGTH_STATE_STATE`).
     - It is kept rather than inlined into the generator so the intersection has its own tests (Task 2).
   - The research proposed filtering on `lock.managed_credential_types`. That would let the generator pick a length the coordinator then refuses.
2. **The generator's own lengths:** a PIN stays 4-12, the range `is_unsafe_pin` is written for. A password is 1-255.
   - No 8-64 floor for passwords (the research's suggestion): the entry's locks decide, and the default is 12.
   - With an entry, the generator's range is intersected with the entry's. An explicit length outside it is refused, naming the range, and so is an empty intersection.
   - Without an entry, only the generator's own range applies.
3. **`generate_credential` returns `{"value": ...}`.**
   - It takes `credential_type`, optional `length`, and an optional `config_entry_id`/`config_entry_title`.
   - `credential_type` is `pin` or `password`. Any other kind is refused with a message, as `set_credential` does.
   - It does not avoid values other users hold: `add_user` and the entity refuse a duplicate (decision 12), and the card can generate again.
4. **The deprecation repair is not fixable and not persistent.**
   - The repo's only deprecation precedent is `number_of_uses`, a config field migrated with an acknowledge-only fix flow (`__init__.py:288-337`). There is no deprecated-service precedent, so this follows Home Assistant's deprecated-service pattern.
   - `generate_pin` raises the issue `generate_pin_deprecated` (severity warning) on every call.
   - Not fixable: an acknowledge flow deletes the issue, and the next automation run raises it again. An issue the user ignores stays ignored when raised again (`issue_registry.async_get_or_create` keeps `dismissed_version`).
   - Not persistent: it clears at the next restart once nothing calls the action.
   - `generate_pin`'s schema and `{"pin": ...}` response are unchanged, so this PR has no Breaking Change section. Removing it in the next major is a breaking change.
5. **`model/pin_generator.py` becomes `model/credential_generator.py`** (research Q4). It is internal, so no shim (memory "back-compat is user-facing only"). Tests and `AGENTS.md:64` move with it.
6. **A type's sync state is `sync_status` alone. No per-type `in_sync`.**
   - The words are those the cards already read in `locks[].sync_status` (`in_sync`, `out_of_sync`, `syncing`, `suspended`), plus `unknown` (being checked). It is `null` when no lock tracks the type for the slot.
   - Why the slot card's Lock Status falls back to `in_sync` today (`slot-card.ts:942-1040`): the sensor attribute omits `unknown`, so a missing `sync_status` is ambiguous there.
   - Here `unknown` is sent, so `in_sync` would only restate `sync_status == "in_sync"`. The review's row icon shows exactly when a type is not `in_sync`.
   - Across locks, a type's state is the furthest from in sync: held, then out of sync, then being checked. It is syncing if any lock is syncing it, unless held. This is the same rule the aggregate sensor uses across types.
7. **A type's value on the slot card is read from its text entity's state**, as the top-level `pin` is today (`websocket.py:976`). So `credentials.pin` and `pin` always agree, and an entity created after the subscription is picked up the same way.
8. **Lock card: per-chip credential states, and the PIN's own `in_sync`, only on a lock that keeps more than PIN.**
   - **What each managed row gains** on such a lock: `credentials: {pin: REDACTED}, password: REDACTED, configured}}`, one entry per type the lock keeps, PIN first.
     - `configured` is whether the user's password text state is non-empty.
     - No password value or length is ever sent, so there is nothing to mask on the lock card.
   - **The row's `in_sync` becomes the PIN's own** status on such a lock, through the shared helper. It is no longer the slot's in-sync sensor, which covers every type.
     - This is the bug fix: today a pending or held password puts the pending clock on the PIN and hides the configured-PIN stand-in (`websocket.py:664-667`, read at `lock-codes-card.ts:732-740` and `:779-781`).
     - It fixes the current card with no TypeScript change.
     - `slots` stays the PIN view, as the spec says.
   - **A PIN-only lock is untouched:** no `credentials` on any row, and `in_sync` still read from the in-sync sensor. Its rows are byte-identical to today's.
   - **No top-level `credential_types`:** a row's `credentials` is the card's signal, and an unused field is not sent. `lock_codes()` is unchanged.
   - Rows keep their current entry attribution. The owner check comes through `slot_sync_state`, which reports nothing (`null`) for a slot another entry owns on the lock.
9. **The entity-tracking test isolates the entity.**
   - A password edit on an enabled user also pushes an update through the lock-change signal and the in-sync sensor, so a test of that would pass with the password entity untracked.
   - The test edits the password of a user who is off, with the websocket's lock signal patched out. With no want changing, `async_want` returns before signalling (`runtime.py:798`).
10. **`KEY_ORDER` is the one TypeScript change in 3a**, with the rebuilt bundle, because Raman listed it here and its contract test (`_BACKEND_KEYS`) is Python. `_BACKEND_KEYS` also gains `password_in_sync`, which the backend already emits.
11. **On this branch alone, every Generate PIN click raises the deprecation repair.**
    - The add-user card keeps calling `generate_pin` until 3b. That is accepted because 3a and 3b ship in the same release (after PR 4).
    - 3b must move the card's PIN generator to `generate_credential` with the entry (`ts/add-user-card.test.ts:293-304` changes; nothing visible does). This is recorded in the 3b carryover (Task 10).

## Payloads 3b reads

```text
subscribe_code_slot event (additions; everything else unchanged, top-level pin/pin_length kept):
  available_types: ["pin", "password"]            # the entry's types, PIN first: one card row each
  credentials: {
    "<type>": {
      value: str | null,  length?: int,            # masked: value null + length; empty: value null, no length
      sync_status: "in_sync"|"out_of_sync"|"syncing"|"suspended"|"unknown" | null
    }, ...                                         # one per available type, in available_types order
  }
  entities.password: str | null                    # the password text entity, for text.set_value; tracked

subscribe_lock_codes event (PIN-only lock: unchanged):
  on a lock that keeps more than PIN, each managed slots[] row:
    in_sync: bool | null                           # the PIN's own sync on this lock (was: every type's)
    credentials: {
      "pin": REDACTED},
      "password": REDACTED, configured: bool}  # never a value or a length
    }

get_config_entry_data result (addition):
  credential_types: ["pin", "password"]           # the entry's types, PIN first

generate_credential(credential_type, length?, config_entry_id? | config_entry_title?) -> {value}
```

Yes, it's a fair concern, and your own rule says to check it: two review rounds full of fixes to earlier fixes mean the design is wrong, not the code. Here are the 2b findings classified. "Other" covers hardening, edge cases and cleanup.

| Round | Real defects in new code | Fixes of earlier fixes | Other | Rejected or repeats |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Per-task reviews | 3: 255-character leak, edit form deciding twice, refused-password gap | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Whole-branch review | 3: lock refusing everything, persisted placeholder, `pin_required` flow | 0 | 2: duplicate-check refactor, leftovers | 4 |
| #1772 review | 1: flat `add_user` | 1: `pin_required` text | 3: unload guard, blank password, cleanup | 5 |

Overall it's converging. Each round found fewer real defects than the last, and most of the latest round was repeats of earlier findings or settled decisions. The defects mostly sit on surface that's genuinely new: a Home Assistant limit I didn't know about, and a config flow that changes under an open dialog. That's what a 20-commit feature PR looks like, not one bad fix being patched over and over.

Two areas do show the pattern you're worried about:

1. **The refused-credential rule (your decision 11) took three passes.** First the hold-only rule left a refused password with no repair. Then a lock refusing everything never turned the user off. The latest review found a third facet: clearing a user's working credential leaves them on with only the refused one. I covered that with "the repair stays raised", not a code fix. A rule that keeps growing exceptions is a design signal. The simple alternative is today's rule: any refused value turns the user off. That costs one thing: a lock refusing a password also cuts off a working PIN. The current rule is fully tested now, though, so keeping it is defensible.
2. **The `pin_required` rename took three fixes:** deleting leftovers at setup, then the acknowledge flow, then the translation. Each round found the next place the old id still lived. That's what renaming a repair id costs. Keeping the id and changing only its text would have needed none of it. It's done now, but I'll keep issue ids from now on.

My recommendation: keep decision 11 as built, unless you'd rather trade the PIN-cut-off cost for the simpler rule.

The branch is `feat/password-config`, in worktree `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/password-config`, HEAD 31cdae3c. The PR puts a user's password in the configuration beside their PIN.

**Why:** four review rounds kept finding new facets of two designs. Raman chose to redesign them rather than patch the facets. Each rework replaces code; it does not add special cases. Delete what the new design makes unnecessary.

## Rework 1: Password entities are reconciled, not tracked per lock event
Today `text.py` adds a slot's Password entity from per-lock events: `register_lock_added_handler`, `register_lock_removed_handler` (with an "exclude the removed lock" rule and a LOADED guard), a `with_password` set, and a discard on slot add. Each event sees the lock set mid-change, and that caused these bugs:
- a reused slot number got no entity back;
- an unload queued removals;
- removing two password locks in one options submit leaves every Password entity behind, because each handler counts the other leaving lock as remaining (`_async_release_locks` calls the handlers before `async_unload_lock` pops the locks);
- a swap of password locks in one update can race the fire-and-forget removal.

**New design:** one reconcile step makes each slot's Password entity match `CredentialType.PASSWORD in available_credential_types(entry)`: add the missing ones, remove the extra ones. It runs once the update pass has settled the lock set and the slots, i.e. after `_async_release_locks` and `_async_setup_new_locks` and after new slots get their standard entities (read `async_update_listener`'s update pass in `__init__.py`). It is the single place that decides, and it is idempotent.
- How the text platform exposes it is your call. A callback registered on the entry's `EntityCallbackRegistry` (the way adders are registered), which the update pass invokes at the end, fits the code's pattern. Removal must be awaited, not fire-and-forget, so an add in the same pass cannot race it.
- Keep: the stored password stays when the entity goes (decision 10); a new slot gets the entity when the entry offers passwords.
- Remove the per-lock handlers, the `with_password` bookkeeping, the LOADED guard and the "exclude the removed lock" logic, if the reconcile makes them unnecessary. Unload must not remove registry entries beyond what the existing slot teardown already does.
- Leave capability changes after setup to PR 4. Make the reconcile a function PR 4 can call when capabilities refresh, and say so in its docstring.

Tests (the existing Password-entity tests must still pass):
- **New:** an entry with two Virtual-type password locks plus the PIN-only mock lock; one options submit removes both password locks; afterwards no slot has a Password entity, and the stored passwords remain. Build two password locks from the existing fixtures (see how `test_the_password_entity_stays_while_a_password_lock_remains` builds a two-lock entry). If a second Virtual lock is impractical, report what you tried rather than writing a test that doesn't reach the case.
- **New:** a swap in one submit, removing the password lock and adding another, leaves exactly one Password entity per slot, with no duplicate unique-id error in `caplog`.
- Mutation: reconcile on per-lock events instead (or skip the reconcile), and the multi-removal test must fail.

## Rework 2: the refusal rule asks one precise question
Read Raman's decision 11, made precise on 2026-10-25, in `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-password-credential-design.md`: "A refused value holds only its own credential, with a repair, while the user has another credential in sync on the refusing lock; otherwise the user is turned off. `slot_disabled` is answered when the user re-enables."

Today `_keeps_another_credential` in `ha/runtime.py` reads the configuration (`coordinator.wants`) with an exception for credentials the same lock holds refused. These kept slipping through:
- a credential the refusing lock doesn't take;
- a suspended (`CANT_SET`) password;
- a not-yet-written one.

**New rule:** when a lock refuses a value for a slot, the user stays on only if another address of that slot on **that lock's worker** has status `IN_SYNC` and a non-None want (a credential actually working there). Replace `_keeps_another_credential`; don't add another exception to it.

**`slot_disabled` is answered when the user re-enables the slot:** delete the `slot_disabled_{entry}_{slot}` issue in the coordinator's successful enable (`async_request_active_toggle(True)`), where `credential_required` is already deleted. Remove the in-sync-based `slot_disabled` deletion from `async_reconcile_issues` (the `wanted` predicate) if nothing else needs it. A repeat refusal raises its own repair again through the normal path. Check the existing `slot_disabled` tests: one that expects deletion once the PIN is back in sync may need to re-enable explicitly. If its scenario no longer makes sense, report it rather than forcing it.

Tests:
- **A suspended password is no fallback:** on the Virtual entry, make the password write fail until it is suspended (`CANT_SET`; see how other tests drive a slot to suspended), then the lock refuses the PIN. The user is turned off.
- **A credential the refusing lock doesn't take is no fallback:** the PIN-only mock lock refuses the PIN of a user who also has a stored password. The user is turned off. If the mock lock fixture makes this hard, use the Virtual entry with the password address absent from the worker.
- **The existing "refused password while the PIN works" test still holds:** the PIN is in sync on that lock, so the user stays on.
- **Re-enable answers `slot_disabled`.** A user whose only credential is refused is turned off with `slot_disabled`. Re-enabling deletes that issue, even if the same PIN is then refused again, which raises a fresh repair through the normal path. Assert the state after each step.
- **Mutations:**
  - Count a non-IN_SYNC address as a fallback: the suspended test must fail.
  - Read the configuration instead of the worker: the doesn't-take test must fail.
  - Drop the enable-time deletion: the re-enable test must fail.

## Fix 3: the edit form decides "offered" once per dialog
`config_flow.py`: `_password_offered` is recomputed each time the edit form is shown, including a re-show after an error. So a password the user cleared can come back if the answer flips between the error and the next submit. Decide it on the first show of the flow only, and keep it for re-shows. Test: patch `_offers_password` to answer True and then False across an error re-show, and assert a cleared password stays cleared. Mutation: recompute on re-show, and the test must fail.

Commit each rework and the fix separately, with test-first where possible. Then run the full suite with `-n auto`. The paced tests `TestPacing`, `test_pins_changed_while_the_lock_is_offline_reach_it_once_each_paced` and `test_a_paced_test_keeps_the_real_delay_between_operations` flake in parallel; re-run any failure on its own. Then run `prek run --all-files`.

In your report, list exactly what code each rework **removed**, as well as what it added. Use the format context.md gives, with SHAs.

## Rework 1: Password entities are reconciled (1f3b8505)

**Removed** (`text.py`):
- The `locks_added` and `lock_removed` handlers and their registrations.
- The `with_password` set, the `add_password_entity` helper and the `discard` on slot add.
- The `ConfigEntryState.LOADED` guard and the "exclude the removed lock" logic.
- The fire-and-forget `config_entry.async_create_task(... async_remove_entity ...)` removal.
- The now-unused imports `ConfigEntryState` and `BaseLock`.
- The standard adder no longer adds the Password entity; it adds only name and PIN.

**Added:**
- `ha/callbacks.py`: `register_entity_reconciler` and `async_reconcile_entities()`. It awaits each registered reconciler in turn and logs one that raises. Its docstring says a capability refresh after setup calls it too, which is the hook for PR 4.
- `text.py`: `reconcile_password_entities()`. It compares the slots that have a Password entity with whether `available_credential_types(entry)` includes passwords. It awaits each removal, then adds the missing entities through the platform's awaitable `async_add_entities` (taken from `entity_platform.async_get_current_platform()`), so an add in the same pass can't race a removal. The stored password stays (decision 10).
- `__init__.py`: one `await callbacks.async_reconcile_entities()` at the end of the update pass, after the locks are released and set up and the new slots have their standard entities. Unload never calls it.

**Tests:**
- New: two Virtual password locks plus the PIN-only mock lock, both password locks removed in one submit. Afterwards no slot has a Password entity and the stored password remains. It failed before the change. A second Virtual lock was easy to build: one more registry entry on the provider entry.
- New: a swap in one submit leaves one live Password entity per slot, with no duplicate unique-id error in `caplog`. It already passed before the change; the race didn't show up in the test harness.
- New: a unit test of the reconciler registry in `tests/test_callbacks.py`.
- Changed: `test_a_second_password_lock_adds_no_second_entity` called the lock-added handler directly, which no longer does anything for text. It is now `test_reconciling_again_adds_no_second_entity` and calls the reconcile twice. Its assertions are unchanged.

**Mutation:** I moved the reconcile from the end of the pass to each lock's removal and arrival. The multi-removal test and `test_the_password_entity_leaves_with_the_last_password_lock` failed. File restored.

## Rework 2: the refusal rule asks the lock's worker (681bf677)

**Removed:**
- `_keeps_another_credential` in `ha/runtime.py`: the configuration read through `coordinator.wants` and the exception for credentials the same lock refused.
- The in-sync `slot_disabled` deletion in `async_reconcile_issues` (the `wanted` predicate). Nothing else needed it.
- `test_a_refusal_is_answered_while_another_types_clear_is_held`, added earlier in this PR.
- `TestSlotRepairs::test_a_refusals_repair_is_answered_beside_a_password_that_wants_nothing` in `tests/providers/virtual/test_e2e.py`. This test is on main (from #1770). Both tests checked that the reconcile answers `slot_disabled`, which no longer happens, so I removed them as scenarios that no longer make sense rather than forcing them.

**Added:**
- `_another_credential_works(worker, address)`: true only if another address of the same slot on that lock's worker has a non-None want and status `IN_SYNC`.
- The coordinator's successful enable (`async_request_active_toggle(True)`) now deletes `slot_disabled_{entry}_{slot}` beside `credential_required`, in one loop that logs a registry failure for either.
- Comments updated in `runtime.py` and `sync/slot.py`.

**Tests** (in `test_password_config.py`; the first three new ones failed before the change):
- A suspended password is no fallback. The password write raises `LockOperationUnsupported`, so it is held `CANT_SET` at once; then the PIN is refused and the user is turned off.
- A credential the refusing lock doesn't take is no fallback. On an entry with Virtual and the PIN-only mock lock, the password is in sync on Virtual and absent from the mock lock's worker; the mock lock refuses the PIN and the user is turned off.
- Re-enable answers `slot_disabled`. Refused PIN: the user is off with the issue. Re-enable: the user is on and the issue is gone. Refused again: the user is off with a fresh issue. I assert after each step.
- The existing "refused password while the PIN works" test still passes.

**Mutations** (files restored after each):

| Mutation | Test that failed |
|---|---|
| Count a non-`IN_SYNC` address as a fallback | the suspended test |
| Read the configuration instead of the worker | the doesn't-take test (and the suspended test) |
| Drop the enable-time deletion | the re-enable test |

## Fix 3: the edit form decides "offered" once per dialog (d14d5398)

**Changed:** `_password_offered` is now `bool | None = None` (it was `bool = False`). `_async_show_reconfigure` computes it only while it is `None`, so a re-show after an error keeps the first answer. A submit with no form drawn still keeps the stored password.

**Test:** `test_a_password_cleared_before_an_error_stays_cleared` in `tests/test_config_flow.py` patches `_offers_password` to answer True then False. The user clears the password and submits a clashing name; the re-shown form still has the field; the corrected submit leaves the password cleared.

**Mutation:** recomputing on every show makes that test fail. File restored.

## Test runs
- Full suite with `-n auto`: 3544 passed, 3 skipped, 14 xfailed. The only failures were the three known paced tests (`TestPacing`, `test_pins_changed_while_the_lock_is_offline_reach_it_once_each_paced`, `test_a_paced_test_keeps_the_real_delay_between_operations`); re-run on their own, all 4 passed.
- `prek run --all-files` passes. Every commit passed prek, including mypy.

## Concerns
- **Re-enabling from the edit form leaves `slot_disabled` behind.** The edit (reconfigure) form writes `enabled: True` without going through `async_request_active_toggle`, so re-enabling there no longer deletes the issue. Before this change the reconcile deletion covered that path. `credential_required` already had the same gap. A single spot that would catch every way of re-enabling is `notify_config_changed` seeing enabled go from off to on; that's a design choice for you to make.
- **A Password entity the user disabled in the registry is never added**, so it never registers for removal, and the reconcile can't remove its registry entry later. The old handlers had the same limit.
- **Later reconcile callers should hold the entry's pass lock.** The update pass calls the reconcile under it; PR 4 calling it on a capability refresh should take it too, to stay serialized with passes.

Mutation scripts are in `/tmp/lcm-rework-mut/`. The main checkout was not touched, and the pre-existing `.entire/.gitignore` change is still unstaged.</result>

Re-enabling from the edit dialog left it open, and `credential_required` already had the same gap. I'm classifying this as a timing issue with the write order — the password gets refused before the PIN is written, so the new user ends up disabled even though the PIN itself is valid. This points to a new facet of the refusal rule: it should apply to another credential on this lock that's wanted and not already held or refused, rather than just checking sync state.

Separately, I'm noting that slot_disabled gets raised when coordinator is None or entry isn't loaded, but then never clears — this is an edge case tied to the rework's slot_disabled change, and could also affect upgrades where a lingering slot_disabled from a previous release on an already re-enabled slot never gets cleared now that reconcile no longer resets it.

Going through the rest of the list: decision 4 is a repeat so I'll reject it; the capability caching/deferred setup item is a known PR4 concern worth checking whether deferred lock setup should trigger reconcile; the add dialog re-deciding offered-per-render is the same facet as the earlier edit-dialog finding, so it's a cheap fix once applied across both; the duplicate-refusal check using config.slots vs config.users is a repeat but worth accepting now given reviewer pushback, switching to config.users minus own name; and the pin_required legacy triple handling could use cleanup around the fix-flow prefix and translation while keeping the deletion logic intact.

Looking at the remaining items—sequential adds being a minor perf gain from batching, and the password_uid duplicate removal format—both seem like small accepts. Tallying things up, I count three real defects this round (the refusal rule timing facet, the narrow slot_disabled clearing, and the add dialog offered-decision sibling), which is fewer than last round's four, suggesting the lifecycle area has converged except for the repeated PR4 item, while the refusal rule keeps surfacing new facets (now six total), signaling it may be inherently too complex and might need a simpler fallback rule instead.

I'm weighing whether to recommend reverting to that simpler rule now: any refusal just turns the user off, with a repair step naming which credential was refused. This would eliminate several accumulated edge cases (another_credential_works, credential_refused, SLOT_DISABLED handling) at the cost of one quirk—a refused password lock also disabling a working PIN until fixed, limited to Virtual until Z-Wave support lands. I think I should present this tradeoff honestly and let the user decide, while also noting that under the simpler rule, the slot_disabled deletion-on-re-enable logic still needs handling for legacy persisted states.

Having both triggers covers the two "answered" cases cleanly — re-enable via transition, legacy via reconcile sync. I'll present this classification to the user along with the recommendation to revert the refusal rule to the simpler version, plus note the additional fix needed.

I should also flag items 5, 6, 8, 9 as minor fixes, and item 4 as worth checking later — specifically whether it's cheap to call reconcile after a deferred lock's setup completes.

The convergence check is in, and the two areas behaved differently:

| Area | This round | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Password entity lifecycle (reworked) | Only #4, capabilities cached late, which is a known PR 4 item. #8 and #9 are small cleanups | **Converged** |
| Refusal rule (reworked) | #1, a **new facet created by the new rule**, and #2, a gap in the new `slot_disabled` clearing | **Not converged.** 6 facets in 5 rounds |
| Edit/add dialog's "offered" decision | #5: the add dialog has the same problem the edit dialog had | Sibling of last round's fix, small |
| Repeats or rejected | #3 (your decision 4, a fourth time), #6 (minor, but reasonable to take), #7 (the legacy handling is needed for entries that never load) | — |

The refusal-rule finding is the telling one. The worker writes a slot's password before its PIN. So when a new user's password is refused, their PIN isn't in sync yet, and "another credential in sync on this lock" says the user has nothing. The user is turned off and the good PIN is never written. An existing user who adds the same bad password keeps working, because their PIN is already in sync. Same input, opposite outcomes, depending on write order.

I could tweak the test again, to "another credential this lock takes, wanted and not held". But every precise version so far has produced a new edge, because "does the user still have something that works?" depends on timing across several addresses.

**My recommendation now: switch to the simple rule.** Any refused value turns the user off, as before #1772. The `slot_disabled` repair already names which credential was refused.
- **What it removes:** the fallback check, the `credential_refused` repair, the extra hold-repair entry, and the facets above. `slot_disabled` goes back to being cleared when the user is re-enabled (the new path) or when everything they want is in sync (the old path, which also covers repairs left by the previous release, #2).
- **What it costs:** on a lock that takes passwords, a refused password also takes away a working PIN until it's fixed. Today that's only Virtual locks; Z-Wave gets passwords in PR 4.

Last turn you chose to keep decision 11, but that was before this round showed the precise version breeding new facets too.

Either way, I'd also take the small ones:
- **#5:** decide "offered" once in the add dialog.
- **#6:** one duplicate rule over every user.
- **#8:** add Password entities concurrently.
- **#9:** share the removal-id format.

3a is unaffected so far. Task 6, the slot card's payload, is still running.

You are simplifying a rule on PR #1772 of Lock Code Manager (a Home Assistant custom integration). The branch is `feat/password-config`, in worktree `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/password-config`, at local HEAD e4fd1159; 31cdae3c is pushed and later commits are local. The PR puts a user's password in the configuration beside their PIN.

First read `/tmp/lcm-pr2b/context.md` (project rules, report format) and follow it, and `/tmp/lcm-pr2b/head.md`. **Never amend; do not push.**

## Main change: the simple refusal rule
Read Raman's revised decision 11 in `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-password-credential-design.md`:

> Any refused value turns the user off, whatever its type; `slot_disabled` names the refused credential, and is answered when the user is re-enabled or once every credential they want is in sync.

The PR first held only the refused credential while another one worked. Six review rounds kept finding new edges, the last one being that the worker writes a slot's password before its PIN, so a new user's refused password turned them off while an existing user's didn't. **Remove that machinery entirely.** Behavior on refusal should match `origin/main` (`git show origin/main:custom_components/lock_code_manager/ha/runtime.py`), except that the `slot_disabled` reason names the refused credential's label instead of always "PIN".

**Remove:**
- `_another_credential_works` and its call in `_on_disable`. `_on_disable` always turns the slot off and raises `slot_disabled`, as on main.
- `Repair.SLOT_DISABLED` from `_HOLD_ISSUES` and the `credential_refused` repair: the `strings.json`/`translations/en.json` block and any handling of it. Check whether anything else references `credential_refused`.
- Comments and docstrings describing the hold-only rule, in `ha/runtime.py`, `sync/slot.py` (the `SLOT_DISABLED` comment) and anywhere else that greps for it.
- The tests for the hold-only behavior in `tests/providers/virtual/test_password_config.py` and elsewhere:
  - a refused password leaving the PIN working;
  - a refused password staying reported once the PIN is cleared;
  - a lock refusing every credential;
  - a suspended password being no fallback;
  - a credential the lock doesn't take being no fallback;
  - a new password lifting the refusal (keep it only if it still tests something under the new rule).

  Replace them with the new rule's tests below.

**`slot_disabled` is answered in two ways:**
1. When the user is re-enabled by any route. This is the coordinator's off-to-on transition, already in place (e4fd1159); keep it.
2. Once every credential the user wants is in sync: restore the reconcile-time deletion in `async_reconcile_issues`, with the multi-type predicate the PR had before the rework (`git show 31cdae3c:custom_components/lock_code_manager/ha/runtime.py`, the `wanted` block): every address of the slot with a non-None want is IN_SYNC, and at least one wants a value. This covers a `slot_disabled` on a slot that was never turned off (no coordinator yet, entry not loaded) and repairs persisted by the previous release.

  Restore `test_a_refusals_repair_is_answered_beside_a_password_that_wants_nothing` (from main's `tests/providers/virtual/test_e2e.py`; it was removed in 681bf677) if it fits this behavior again.

**Keep:** hold repairs (`slot_suspended`, `slot_clear_failed`) passing the `credential` placeholder is harmless; leave it. The `DuplicateCodeError(credential=...)` label stays.

**New tests** (Virtual entry, `lcm_config_entry`):
- **A refused password turns the user off even while the PIN works.** Patch the Virtual set to refuse passwords; see the existing `_refuse_passwords` helper if it survives, or write one. The user ends up disabled, and `slot_disabled` names "Password".
- **A new user with a PIN and a refused password is turned off,** the same outcome as an existing user. This is the write-order case that motivated the change.
- **`slot_disabled` is answered by sync without a re-enable:** raise it on a slot that stays enabled (for example, create the issue directly, or call `_on_disable` with no coordinator), and once the slot is in sync the issue is deleted.
- **Mutations:**
  - Restore a fallback check, so `_on_disable` returns early when the PIN is in sync: the first test must fail.
  - Drop the reconcile deletion: the sync test must fail.

## Small fixes (one commit each, test-first)
1. **The add dialog decides "offered" once per flow,** as the edit dialog now does (`config_flow.py` `async_step_one`; see `_password_offered` in the reconfigure path). Test: patch `_offers_password` True then False across an error re-show of the add form; a typed password still reaches the created user. Mutation: re-decide per render.
2. **One duplicate rule over every user.** `_refuse_duplicate` in `ha/slot_coordinator.py` builds the other users from `config.slots`, which leaves out users with no slot number. Use `config.users` minus this slot's user name (`config.name_for(self._slot_num)`) with the shared `credential_holder`. Test: a user record without a slot number holds PIN 1234, and setting 1234 on another user through the coordinator is refused. Building an unnumbered user: see `unnumbered_user_subentry` in `tests/common.py`.
3. **Add Password entities concurrently.** `text.py`'s reconcile awaits `async_add_entities` per slot in turn. Run the adds concurrently (a `TaskGroup`, as `invoke_entity_removers_for_slot` does for removals), keeping removals awaited before adds. The existing tests are the check.
4. **Share the removal-id format.** `text.py`'s `_password_uid` repeats `BaseLockCodeManagerEntity._get_removal_uid`'s `f"{slot_num}|{key}"`. Put the format in one module-level helper in `entity.py`, used by both.

Then run the full suite with `-n auto`. The paced tests `TestPacing`, `test_pins_changed_while_the_lock_is_offline_reach_it_once_each_paced` and `test_a_paced_test_keeps_the_real_delay_between_operations` flake in parallel; re-run any failure on its own. Then `prek run --all-files`.

In your report, list what code was **removed** and what was added, and give the SHAs. Use the format context.md gives.

Two agents are now working, one per PR, in separate worktrees:

- **#1772, the simple refusal rule.** Any refused value turns the user off, as before #1772, and the `slot_disabled` repair names which credential was refused.

  - **New tests:** a refused password turns the user off even while the PIN works. A new user and an existing user get the same outcome, which is the write-order case that triggered this. Each fix gets a mutation check.
  - **Same batch:** the four small fixes:
    - the add dialog decides once whether to show the Password field;
    - one duplicate rule covers every user;
    - Password entities are added concurrently;
    - the entity removal key format is defined in one place.
- **3a Task 7, the lock card chips.** Each managed chip gets each credential type's state, and its PIN state stops reflecting the password. Its fix test must fail on today's code first, and PIN-only locks must come out byte-identical. I told it to create a held password through a failed write rather than a refusal, so it won't conflict with the simple rule once 3a is rebased onto #1772.

3a Task 6, the slot card's payload, landed cleanly. Its four mutations each failed their named test, including the one showing a masked payload never carries the password.

When the #1772 change lands, I'll run one more review of it as the convergence check.

3. **d137af67** `perf(text)`: the Password entity adds run concurrently in an `asyncio.TaskGroup`, after the removals are awaited. The existing tests pass.
4. **21ed9883** `refactor(entity)`: a module-level `removal_uid(slot_num, key)` in `entity.py` is used by `BaseLockCodeManagerEntity._get_removal_uid` and by `text.py`. `_password_uid` is removed.

  - `TestPacing::test_writes_at_startup_are_spaced`
  - `test_pins_changed_while_the_lock_is_offline_reach_it_once_each_paced`
  - `test_a_paced_test_keeps_the_real_delay_between_operations`

  Re-run on their own, all 4 tests passed.
- **`prek run --all-files`:** clean. Every commit also passed `prek` with mypy.

- The new-user test adds the user through `SERVICE_ADD_USER` and finds the slot with `get_entry_config(...).assignment.slot("Guest")`.
- The unnumbered-user test builds its own `MockConfigEntry` (version 5), following the pattern in `test_services.py`.</result>

input.message:
The convergence review of 21ed9883 found no new problem in the refusal rule or the entity lifecycle: those reworks hold. Please fix the small items it found, in new commits (no amend, no push), test-first where behavior changes:

1. **Edit-flow exemption against normalized data** (`config_flow.py`, around 1368). The "unchanged value isn't re-checked" comparison uses raw `subentry.data`, so a legacy PIN stored with padding (`' 1234'`) never matches its own stripped submission, and a rename is refused as `pin_not_unique` when another user holds `1234`. Compare against the normalized stored user (`get_entry_config(entry).users[held]`, which strips) instead. Test: legacy padded PIN plus another user with the same stripped PIN; renaming the first user succeeds.
2. **Name the colliding user in the YAML duplicate error.** `pin_not_unique` and `password_not_unique` are returned with `{"name": name}` from the pasted-users path, but the strings don't use `{name}`. Either make the pasted-users errors use their own keys with `{name}` in the text (e.g. `pin_not_unique_in_block`: "{name} has a PIN another user already has."), leaving the form's field errors as they are, or another clean way. Keep both string files identical.
3. **An empty password in YAML means none,** as an empty PIN does. `USER_SCHEMA`'s password validator refuses `""` as blank. Make `""` mean "no password" in the YAML path (dropped or stored empty, consistently with how an empty PIN is treated there), while a whitespace-only non-empty password is still refused. Test both.
4. **Clearing a type the user doesn't hold writes nothing.** `async_request_credential_update(type, "")` on a user without that credential writes `{type: ''}` and runs an update pass. Skip the write when the stored value is already empty and nothing else would change. Test: `clear_credential(password)` on a PIN-only user leaves the subentry data unchanged (no `password` key added).
5. **Remove the unused `credential` placeholder** on hold repairs (`ha/runtime.py` around 991), and revert the `_` → `address` unpack if nothing else needs it. No translation uses it any more.
6. **Lower-case "password" in prose.** Messages insert `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` mid-sentence ("bob already has this Password", "'carol' cannot have the Password 'bob' already has", "refused the Password for slot 3", "Password length 3 is not accepted"). Use a lower-case noun mid-sentence; "PIN" stays "PIN". Keep the label where it starts a sentence. One small helper, not ad-hoc `.lower()` calls. Update the tests that match these strings.
7. **Diagnostics: one loop over the managed types** instead of two hand-written blocks in `_slot_diagnostic`. Same output keys (`pin`, `password`).
8. **`async_reconcile_issues`: compute each address's status once,** and derive both `in_sync` and the wanted-in-sync predicate from it.
9. **Docstrings that promise a reconcile on capability changes.** The `async_reconcile_entities` docstring in `ha/callbacks.py` and `available_credential_types`' ("a lock not set up yet adds its types when it is") claim something nothing does yet. Make them say what happens now (the update pass reconciles), and that PR 4 calls the reconcile when capabilities change.

Then run the full suite with `-n auto` (the paced flakes as before) and `prek run --all-files`, and report with SHAs.

I'm reconsidering whether the length-bounds check has a real bug: it counts locks that advertise a credential type even if they're not actually writable, so a Z-Wave lock that can't receive passwords could wrongly block a valid 12-character password for other locks.

The fix is to filter the length-bounds helper by managed credential types so both the generator and coordinator stay consistent. Separately, the lock card's in-sync indicator can show stale "True" on an offline lock in multi-type mode, so I should gate it on lock availability the same way the sensor does.

On furthest_sync_state, aggregating "syncing" across locks when one is just backing off from out_of_sync could be misleading, but ranking per-lock words (in_sync < syncing < out_of_sync) would change existing sensor aggregation semantics too. I'll skip that change since it's consistent with how the sensor already aggregates.

The 'unknown' vocabulary decision is already explicit and the card handles it — just a minor docstring fix needed. More importantly, I spot a real bug: the add-user card sends a default length of 4 even when an entry requires a minimum of 6, which will fail. The fix is to only send length if the user actually changed it, letting the service fall back to its own default and clamp into the valid range — that's worth accepting. I also want to reconsider the two in_sync sources, since unifying them might break PIN-only locks that still need their own branch.

Actually there's a risk: the existing test manipulates sensor state independently of the worker to prove the PIN-only path reads the sensor directly, so unifying would break that test's assumption rather than real behavior. I'll instead fix the per-type path to follow the same availability gate as the sensor, keeping the branch separate and preserving PIN-only behavior, and skip the riskier unification. Next I want to check the slot_addresses quadratic performance concern, since Z-Wave locks can have up to 250 slots realistically.

The quadratic cost only matters for managed slots since those are the ones serialized and synced, and typical setups rarely exceed 30 users, so I'll accept it as a minor issue with a cheap grouping fix possible later. The comprehension style and dead guard items are fine to accept as-is, and I'll keep available_types alongside credentials keys since the design review favored an explicit order contract over relying on dict ordering. So the real defects worth fixing are items 1, 2, and 5, with 7, 8, and 9 as minor cleanups, plus a docstring fix still pending.

I'll finalize fixing items 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and skip 3, 6, 10, then hand this off to the Task 10 agent that already has the branch context.

Review found three real defects: password length range wrongly including Z-Wave locks, PIN status ignoring offline state, and the add-user card always sending a default length of 4. I'll fix those plus four minor issues (#4, #7, #8, #9), while skipping #3, #6, and #10 as not worth changing.

input.message:
I ran the whole-branch review of b0ddb45b. Please fix these in new commits (no amend, no push), test-first where behavior changes, each with a mutation check (restore in `finally`):

1. **Length bounds only from locks that keep the type.** `credential_length_bounds` (`ha/entry.py`) counts every lock advertising a type, including ones Lock Code Manager never writes it to. Z-Wave maps a password capability into `cached_capabilities` but doesn't write passwords until PR 4. So a mixed entry's password range, used both by `generate_credential` and by the slot coordinator's length check, is narrowed by a lock that never receives a password. Filter on `credential_type in lock.managed_credential_types`. Both callers use the helper, so the generator and the check stay consistent. Test: the Virtual lock (unbounded password) plus a lock that advertises a password range but doesn't keep passwords. The generator's default stays 12, and a 12-character password is accepted by the coordinator. The mock lock with a patched capability cache may do; check how its `managed_credential_types` comes out. While there, write it as a comprehension (finding 8).
2. **The lock card's PIN `in_sync` respects availability on multi-type locks.** In `_serialize_lock_coordinator`'s per-type branch (websocket.py ~786), `in_sync` comes straight from the worker. A PIN-only lock reads the in-sync sensor, which is unavailable while the lock entity is, so `in_sync` is omitted there. A password lock reports a stale True, and the card shows the configured PIN as confirmed on an offline lock. Make the per-type branch report nothing (`None`, as the sensor path does) under the same conditions the sensor is unavailable. Read how the in-sync binary sensor decides availability, and check the case before the lock first answers. Keep PIN-only rows byte-identical. Test: Virtual lock entity unavailable, so the chip's `in_sync` is None. Mutation: drop the gate.
3. **The add-user card doesn't force its default length.** `ts/add-user-card.ts` (~515) always sends its length (default 4) to `generate_credential`, so on an entry whose locks need at least 6, the first Generate fails. Send `length` only once the user has set one, and let the action fit its own default otherwise. Look at how the card holds its length field. Tests in `ts/add-user-card.test.ts`: an untouched length isn't sent; a chosen length is. Rebuild the bundle in the same commit.
4. **`slot_addresses` scans every tracked address per call.** The serializers call it per slot, per type and per lock on every signal. Group the worker's addresses by slot once per serialization, or give the helper a cheaper path; your call, as long as the shared helper's callers stay correct. The existing tests are the check.
5. **The dead guard:** the `if slot_ids else None` at websocket.py ~794 can't be false. Remove it.
6. **The docstring claim.** `slot_sync_state`'s docstring claims the per-type payload and the sensor never disagree, but the payload sends `unknown`, which the sensor attribute omits. Make the docstring say exactly how they relate.

Not taking: the aggregate's syncing-versus-out-of-sync ranking (it's the sensors' rule), merging the two `in_sync` sources (it would change PIN-only payloads), and dropping `available_types` (it's the explicit ordered contract for 3b).

Then:
- re-run the full suite, coverage against 2b's tip, vitest and `prek run --all-files`;
- in `/tmp/lcm-pr3a/pr-body.md`, describe fixes 1-3 where they belong (the length rule, the lock card, the add-user card);
- add back a "Mutation checks: each rule was broken on purpose, and a named test failed every time" line. Every task report and these fixes confirm it.

Report with SHAs.

I ran the whole-branch review of b0ddb45b. Please fix these in new commits (no amend, no push), test-first where behavior changes, each with a mutation check (restore in `finally`):

1. **Length bounds only from locks that keep the type.** `credential_length_bounds` (`ha/entry.py`) counts every lock advertising a type, including ones Lock Code Manager never writes it to. Z-Wave maps a password capability into `cached_capabilities` but doesn't write passwords until PR 4. So a mixed entry's password range, used both by `generate_credential` and by the slot coordinator's length check, is narrowed by a lock that never receives a password. Filter on `credential_type in lock.managed_credential_types`. Both callers use the helper, so the generator and the check stay consistent. Test: the Virtual lock (unbounded password) plus a lock that advertises a password range but doesn't keep passwords. The generator's default stays 12, and a 12-character password is accepted by the coordinator. The mock lock with a patched capability cache may do; check how its `managed_credential_types` comes out. While there, write it as a comprehension (finding 8).
2. **The lock card's PIN `in_sync` respects availability on multi-type locks.** In `_serialize_lock_coordinator`'s per-type branch (websocket.py ~786), `in_sync` comes straight from the worker. A PIN-only lock reads the in-sync sensor, which is unavailable while the lock entity is, so `in_sync` is omitted there. A password lock reports a stale True, and the card shows the configured PIN as confirmed on an offline lock. Make the per-type branch report nothing (`None`, as the sensor path does) under the same conditions the sensor is unavailable. Read how the in-sync binary sensor decides availability, and check the case before the lock first answers. Keep PIN-only rows byte-identical. Test: Virtual lock entity unavailable, so the chip's `in_sync` is None. Mutation: drop the gate.
3. **The add-user card doesn't force its default length.** `ts/add-user-card.ts` (~515) always sends its length (default 4) to `generate_credential`, so on an entry whose locks need at least 6, the first Generate fails. Send `length` only once the user has set one, and let the action fit its own default otherwise. Look at how the card holds its length field. Tests in `ts/add-user-card.test.ts`: an untouched length isn't sent; a chosen length is. Rebuild the bundle in the same commit.
4. **`slot_addresses` scans every tracked address per call.** The serializers call it per slot, per type and per lock on every signal. Group the worker's addresses by slot once per serialization, or give the helper a cheaper path; your call, as long as the shared helper's callers stay correct. The existing tests are the check.
5. **The dead guard:** the `if slot_ids else None` at websocket.py ~794 can't be false. Remove it.
6. **The docstring claim.** `slot_sync_state`'s docstring claims the per-type payload and the sensor never disagree, but the payload sends `unknown`, which the sensor attribute omits. Make the docstring say exactly how they relate.

Not taking: the aggregate's syncing-versus-out-of-sync ranking (it's the sensors' rule), merging the two `in_sync` sources (it would change PIN-only payloads), and dropping `available_types` (it's the explicit ordered contract for 3b).

This is the fifth time reviewers have flagged decision 4 — a stored value counts even if no current lock accepts its type. That persistence makes me wonder if the decision itself is the problem, even though it was Raman's explicit call. I should note how often this keeps resurfacing and consider offering to revisit it.

The edit dialog hides a stored password with no way to clear it, which could lead to a stuck error if a hand-edited invalid value blocks the form from submitting. This is really a consequence of decisions 4 and 10 combining — a hidden credential keeps the user enabled and uneditable — so a narrow fix might be to skip validation on a carried-but-not-offered password.

Capability changes are a repeat from PR4, and the lack of length checks in add_user/forms is also a known pre-existing gap for PINs — but now it's worse, since under the simpler rule a rejected password disables the whole slot. Adding a length check using the credential_length_bounds helper seems like a cheap fix worth considering.

The disabled password entity never being removed is a known carryover, and set iteration order causing nondeterministic duplicate reporting is a real, small issue fixable by iterating credential types in a fixed order (PIN before PASSWORD).

I'm also working through the slot_disabled logic with its two rules and the cross-lock deletion scenario — tracing through whether a race actually exists between lock A raising slot_disabled and lock B's sync deleting it, and concluding that because disable is eager/synchronous, wants become empty immediately, so the deletion predicate never fires and the race doesn't actually happen. The _TOKEN_PREFIX parallel list is a minor cleanup risk (KeyError if a new credential type is added) — worth a cheap coverage test rather than a bigger refactor. The hard-coded 255 in strings is low-value, so I'll skip addressing it.

content.thinking:
I need to update the spec and dispatch an agent with the details of how the credential-required rule should only count credential types that are actually offered to the user—checking the coordinator's enable logic, auto-disable on clear, and the config flow's handling of subentry versus setup flows where PIN or password availability differs.

The setup flow complicates things since there's no runtime yet to know which locks offer which credential types; I'm leaning toward treating unknown offerings leniently at setup (count all types) and letting the coordinator's runtime rule catch mismatches later, though that means a password-only user on PIN-only locks could stay enabled until cleared. The core semantics I want: a user can be enabled only if they hold a credential type that at least one lock in the entry actually supports.

Simpler path: since the setup form only offers a PIN field anyway (no Password field at setup), I can just say setup only considers PIN-type users, refusing enabled users who only have passwords with a "needs a PIN" message, and letting them add passwords after setup completes.

Now I'm wondering about users who become credential-less after a password lock is removed. Rather than having the update pass silently disable them, it might be cleaner to fold "has an offered credential" into the active-state computation itself, so a slot with no viable credential type is simply treated as inactive and all lock values clear — though that requires recomputing active status whenever locks change, which feels like it could be overengineering this.

I'll keep scope minimal and match what was actually requested: a credential only counts if some lock in the entry accepts its type, applied specifically to the enable-toggle and auto-disable-on-clear paths, not a broader recompute. The remaining edge case (a password lock disappearing later) stays out of scope and goes into the carryover notes. The places to touch are the active-toggle request handler using offered types, the auto-disable-on-clear logic checking remaining offered types, the config flow's slot-enabled-without-credential check (using available credential types from subentries, or PIN-only in the setup flow), and the add_users service using the entry's offered types.

Schema-level validation (enabled_requires_credential in USERS_SCHEMA) can't know about offered types since it runs without entry context, so that check needs to move into the post-parse YAML validation step instead. I also realize the newly-added "carried password" credential type must now only count if it's offered — meaning a user whose sole credential is a stored password on a non-password entry would fail the credential check while enabled, which actually reverses the expected test behavior I noted earlier. I'll add a helper function, has_offered_credential, taking a user and the offered credential types, placed in model/config.py, and update decision 4 in the spec accordingly.

content.text: You chose to count only the types the entry offers. Recording it as a revision of decision 4, then dispatching the change. The three small fixes landed first, as 1f5cc403, eebb6bf5 and 3d83bbf7.

Until now, any stored credential counted, so a user could be enabled, or stay enabled after their PIN was cleared, holding only a password no lock in the entry takes.

Add one helper in `model/config.py` beside `credential_values` and `has_credential`. For example, `has_credential(user, offered)` gains an `offered: Collection[CredentialType]` argument, or a new `has_offered_credential(user, offered)`. 2. **Coordinator clear:** `async_request_credential_update(type, "")` auto-disables an enabled user when no other credential of an offered type remains.
3. **Config flow:**
   - In the subentry add and edit dialogs, the offered types are `available_credential_types(entry)` when the entry is loaded, and PIN only otherwise.

   - The carried password from 1f5cc403 is by definition a type the entry doesn't offer, so it no longer counts toward the rule. A password-only user on such an entry, edited while enabled, is now refused `missing_credential_if_enabled`. Update the test from 1f5cc403 that expects this edit to succeed, and say so in your report.
4. **`add_user` service** (`ha/services.py` `async_add_users`): an enabled user needs a credential of an offered type.

Keep the stored password everywhere (decision 10): nothing deletes it.

On the PIN-only mock entry (`lock_code_manager_config_entry` + `mock_lock_config_entry`), where passwords are not offered:

On the Virtual entry (`lcm_config_entry`), where passwords are offered, the existing tests already cover a password-only user being enabled. Make sure they still pass unchanged.

**Setup flow:** pasted YAML with an enabled password-only user is refused.

**Mutations**, each failing a named test:
- Count every stored type in the coordinator enable check.
- Count every stored type in the clear check.
- Count every stored type in `add_user`.

- Update the PR description draft `/tmp/lcm-pr2b/pr-body.md`. The "A user needs a PIN or a password to be enabled" bullet must say: a credential counts only if a lock in the entry takes its type; a stored password is kept but doesn't count while no lock takes passwords; and the setup flow offers PIN only.
- Run the affected tests, then the full suite with `-n auto`. The paced tests `TestPacing`, `test_pins_changed_while_the_lock_is_offline_reach_it_once_each_paced` and `test_a_paced_test_keeps_the_real_delay_between_operations` flake in parallel; re-run any failure on its own.
- Run `prek run --all-files`.
- Report with SHAs, including any existing test whose expected value changed and why.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that set_credential's enable_if_disabled path raises a raw CredentialRequiredError, which should be wrapped as a ServiceValidationError instead — storing the credential first then failing on enable is acceptable since it's consistent with "kept". I'm also checking the auto-disable branch that runs before the no-op return, since it affects whether a credential gets cleared.

Clearing a non-held credential currently disables a password-only user even when none was offered, which is wrong under the inactive-state rule — the fix is to add a no-op check before that disable logic runs.

For orphaned registry rows (both the carryover disabled-entity case and the new failed-reauth case), I think the cleaner fix is to have reconcile remove registry rows directly by their unique ids from the entity registry rather than going through the loaded-entity remover — that approach closes both cases at once.

I'm now weighing the slot_disabled cross-lock deletion issue that occurs when the coordinator doesn't exist yet during setup, which is a narrower case since there's no eager disable happening without a coordinator present.

Since coordinators are actually created before locks are set up, this timing scenario can't occur and I'm rejecting it.

Looking at startup more carefully: before locks are set up, offered types are empty, causing password-only users to briefly go inactive and the active sensor to flap off-then-on, which could trigger unwanted automations or a spurious enable-during-window refusal. The fix would be to treat the offered state as unknown until locks have settled, using a runtime flag set after the first setup pass completes, so the credential gate isn't applied prematurely.

For the enabling-during-window issue, the same settling flag would let that check be skipped leniently during startup — accepting this as a real fix.

The capability cache issue and duplicate rule repeat earlier findings, so I'm skipping those. The tri-state flag is just cleanup, also skipping.

For performance, caching the offered types set on runtime_data and updating it whenever locks change or the setup pass completes would solve both the startup flapping issue and the recomputation overhead together — accepting this as a combined fix.

So the real defects are the inactive-sensor startup flap, the enable-during-window race, case 2 of the duplicate rule, and the capability cache timing — with the first three all stemming from the same inactive/decision-4 rework, which is a pattern I'm noticing recur across these facets.

I think these three facets are a natural, bounded consequence of the decision-4 change rather than a sign of fixes breeding more fixes — they're coherent to resolve together via the cached offered-types design with startup leniency. I'll report to the user that convergence regressed specifically because of this new decision-4 surface, recommend the fix, and note that reverting decision 4 would just invite the same complaints from reviewers again — then dispatch the fix agent and explain the classification afterward.

content.text:
This round reopened the convergence question. Three of the real defects are new edges of the decision 4 change I just made:

| Finding | Class |
|---|---|
| **#1** `set_credential` with `enable_if_disabled` on an entry whose locks take no passwords fails with an "Unknown error" after storing the password | **Decision 4 facet** |
| **#2** Clearing a credential the user doesn't hold now turns off a password-only user. That stops them coming back automatically when a password lock returns | **Decision 4 facet**, from a change the agent flagged and I accepted |
| **#5** At every restart the offered types are empty until the locks are set up. Password-only users briefly read inactive, the active sensor flaps, and enabling one in that window is refused with a lasting repair | **Decision 4 facet** |
| **#3** Password registry rows that never load (a user-disabled entity, or a lock dropped by reauth) are never cleaned up | Partly new |
| **#9** Offered types are recomputed over every lock on every condition change | Performance |
| #6 capabilities, #7 duplicate rule, #8 tri-state flag | Repeats or cleanup |
| #4 an unrelated lock clearing `slot_disabled` while the coordinator doesn't exist yet | Rejected: coordinators are created before any lock is set up, so that window doesn't exist |

These three facets come from the first review after decision 4 grew a runtime rule, so they're new surface rather than the old clusters. Two share one cause: nothing records whether the entry's locks have settled. One coherent fix covers #5 and #9:
- **Cache the offered types** on the entry's runtime data, updated where locks are held and released.
- **Leave them unknown until the first update pass settles.** While unknown, neither the inactive gate nor the enable check applies, so startup can't flap or refuse.

The other fixes:
- **#2:** check the no-op before the auto-disable.
- **#1:** wrap the enable error as a validation error.
- **#3:** reconcile Password entities against the entity registry rather than only the loaded ones, which removes orphaned rows of any origin.

content.text:
I pushed #1772 at 726f8eb4, which includes the inactive rule. The review after it found three new edges of the decision 4 change:
- **Unknown error:** `set_credential` with `enable_if_disabled` fails with an "Unknown error" when no lock takes passwords.
- **Clearing turns users off:** clearing a credential a user doesn't hold turns off a password-only user, so they don't come back by themselves.
- **Startup:** on every restart, password-only users briefly read inactive, their active sensor flaps, and enabling one in that window is refused with a persistent repair.

These are new surface, not the old clusters coming back. Two of them, the startup one and a performance finding, share one cause: nothing records whether the entry's locks have finished setting up.

An agent is fixing all of it as one design rather than separate patches:
- **Cached offered types:** the credential types the entry's locks take are stored once, and stay unknown until the first update pass has set up the locks. While they're unknown, neither the inactive rule nor the enable check applies, so restarts can't flap a sensor or refuse an enable.
- **The other fixes:**
  - clearing a credential the user doesn't hold does nothing again;
  - the enable failure becomes a normal validation error;
  - Password entities are reconciled against the entity registry, so leftover rows are removed too, such as a user-disabled one or one stranded by reauth.

Each fix comes with tests and mutation checks.

The 3a rebase onto 726f8eb4 is still running and will need one more rebase after this. When the fix lands I'll push and review #1772 again. If that round finds nothing new in decision 4, it has converged.
